title: Runtime adapter handoffs and routing scenarios
content:
Purpose:
This working note sketches concrete ownership handoffs and routing-scenario playbooks for the control plane surface: API gateway, orchestrator, and runtime adapters. The intent is pragmatic: give engineers oncall and integration owners clear checklists for common routing decisions and multi-region degradations, plus a lightweight decision canvas to accelerate design reviews.

Scope and assumptions:
- Scope: request routing policies and ownership boundaries affecting control plane components (gateway, orchestrator, runtime adapters / runtime pools). Not covering low-level kernel or model optimization details.
- Assumes: unified control-plane API exists for route config; runtime adapters expose capability metadata (latency profile, cost tier, region, model variants).
- Goal: operational clarity for 95th-percentile SLOs during normal and degraded conditions.

Key components and responsibilities (brief):
- API Gateway (edge): public ingress, auth, per-tenant quotas, coarse routing rules (region affinity, tier selection). Owner: edge/gateway team.
- Orchestrator (control-plane decision engine): evaluates route policy expressions, capacity-aware placement, rollout logic, multi-region fallback. Owner: platform orchestrator team.
- Runtime Adapters (runtimes): adapters report capabilities and accept directed traffic; own adapter-level health, scaling, and local fallbacks. Owners: serving-runtime subteams per adapter family (cuda-adapter, cpu-quant-adapter, private-vpc-adapter).
- Observability & Tracing: shared but instrumented; tracing hook owned by observability team with per-route dashboards surfaced to owners.

Ownership handoff canvas (one-page checklist for design/integration):
- Oncall owners: gateway-team, orchestrator-team, adapter-team(s)
- Schema compatibility: who validates adapter capability schema; adapter owner confirms breaking-change window
- Fallback semantics: who implements and owns fallback logs and metric alerts
- Rollout gates: who configures canary thresholds and automatic rollback
- Security boundary: who owns auth/token exchange for private adapters
- Runbook link: pointer to per-adapter runbook and SLOs

Routing policy scenarios (concrete examples and owner decisions):
1) Latency-first routing (customer-facing chat widget)
   - Policy: prefer region-local runtime with latency <= 60ms p95, otherwise fallback to nearest compatible region, otherwise degrade model to low-cost small variant.
   - Implementation notes: Gateway applies region affinity header; orchestrator evaluates adapter health + latency windows and returns route token; adapter owner provides latency SLA.
   - Ownership: orchestrator owns policy evaluation; gateway owns affinity header enforcement; adapter owner owns accuracy of reported latency metrics.

2) Cost-first batch embedding pipeline
   - Policy: route to cheapest compatible adapter in the same cloud region unless backlog < 3s, then expand to cross-region low-cost pool.
   - Implementation notes: orchestrator must be able to compute cost score from adapter metadata and consider queue depth. Adapter owners must expose per-token cost estimate.
   - Ownership: orchestrator implements scoring; cost estimates certified by finance/serving-runtime; gateway passes route flags for billing.

3) Privacy-first (PII / regulated tenant)
   - Policy: always route to private VPC adapter in tenant region; if unavailable, block and escalate (no cross-region fallback).
   - Implementation notes: gateway tags request with tenant policy; orchestrator enforces strict constraint.
   - Ownership: security/compliance owns policy; private-adapter owners ensure KMS/HSM integrations and attestations.

4) Degraded capacity multi-region fallback
   - Policy: if local capacity exhausted and latency budget violated, orchestrator attempts regional fallback chain: local replica -> cold spare in same region -> nearest region warm spare -> global fallback on reduced model variant.
   - Implementation notes: orchestrator must carry graceful downgrade plan and notify gateway to signal degraded mode to client (429 vs 200-with-degraded-info).
   - Ownership: orchestrator owns fallback choreography; adapter owners own warm/cold spare readiness and scaling hooks.

Handoff checklists (adapter -> orchestrator) before integration:
- Capability contract (JSON schema) verified and checked into repo
- Metrics emitted: p50/p95 latency, qlen, token-cost, health-status, model-variant-id
- Health semantics: what does transient vs sustained failure look like? (thresholds)
- Warmup behavior: cold-start latency and warmup signal
- Auth handshake: token exchange and TLS cert rotation cadence
- Test harness: synthetic load test that orchestrator can run as part of onboarding

Runbook excerpts (short):
- Adapter degraded: if adapter p95 > 2x baseline for >5m, orchestrator will mark as overloaded and begin routing away. Pager: adapter oncall (P1).
- Orchestrator decision loop failure: if orchestrator fails to respond to gateway in SLA (100ms median), gateway should return local cached route or apply static fallback and generate incident alert for orchestrator oncall.
- Gateway auth failure: gateway returns 401 and no routing decision is made; security oncall paged.

Decision matrix (how we pick owner for cross-cutting changes):
- Small, adapter-local change (metrics, minor schema): adapter owner approves
- Routing policy change affecting multiple regions: orchestrator + gateway + affected adapter owners sign-off
- Security/compliance-affecting change: security/compliance + orchestrator sign-off required

Observability and SLOs to add (proposed):
- Route decision latency (gateway->orchestrator roundtrip) p50/p95/p999
- Cross-region failover time (time from overload detection to traffic draining)
- Adapter accuracy of advertised cost/latency (drift % over 24h)
- In-flight downgrade rate (percentage of requests served by downgraded model variant)

Open questions / trade-offs to resolve in next design review:
- Centralized vs decentralized policy authoring: one policy language makes audits easier, but team autonomy suffers. Proposal: central language + adapter-local extensions.
- How to certify adapter-reported cost estimates? (periodic reconciliation job vs billing sampling)
- Should gateway expose a standardized degraded-mode response payload that apps can rely on?

Next steps and action items:
- (Liam) prototype orchestrator scoring function for cost-first scenario (due 2025-01-10)
- (Sofia) draft capability schema PR and adapter onboarding checklist (due 2024-12-01)
- (Diego) add route-level tracing annotations and sample dashboards (due 2024-12-15)
- Follow-up design review scheduled: platform-arch sync 2024-12-05

Appendix: quick links and refs
- Design PR: GH:github.com/redwood-inference/platform/orchestrator#412
- Incident runbook template: Confluence:cp-routing-handbook
- Onboarding checklist: JIRA:PLAT-1890

Notes: this is a working draft. Expect evolving fields and schema as adapters are onboarded. Use this as the canonical handoff checklist until a formal playbook is published in Confluence.
